rv.q: The brilliance of Suzan-Lori Parks’s eviscerating new play White Noise is that underneath the finely crafted, often sharply funny apparent realism of its surface, its roots stretch deep away into archetype.
Every time Ms. Parks writes a play, she seems to come up with a brand-new genre.
That doesn't mean that the play and the queasy complicity it demands won't provoke or disturb you.
But it takes a nosedive in the sloppy second half, confounding the assured direction of Oskar Eustis and the best efforts of a small, ace cast headed by the magnetic Daveed Diggs.
But it's hard not to wish that White Noise had pinned them down more effectively.

The genius of White Noise isn’t simply in the idea; it’s in where Parks—and her tight-knit cast, guided by Public artistic director Oskar Eustis—takes it, and she takes it to some very, very disturbing places.
For Parks, too, it’s an all-pins-flying strike.
The production is intense, the performances brave and persuasive.
White Noise operates on so many different levels at once, that it leaves you ruminating on what you saw days later, which is generally true of only the finest plays.
It's necessary to have artists like Suzan-Lori Parks around to keep us thinking, and talking, about what we can aspire to be.

rv.q: White Noise is, ultimately, about facing what is: no resolution, not even a lot of hope, a great deal of bitter irony and grief–but the possibility of change.

White Noise is both a thought-provoking and thoughtful examination of racism, and the vexed politics of race and identity that have tested interracial relations personally and politically to so many breaking points.
It is allegory delivered by gut-punch, at a time when the urgency of such forcefulness is in high demand.
Notwithstanding its far-fetched and questionable concept, 'White Noise' (which runs exactly three hours in length) is mostly engrossing and provocative.
While the sexual plot twists sometimes make White Noise feel like a highbrow soap opera, it also feels like a microcosm of American society...
The provocative wager between Leo and Ralph — no spoilers here about its nature — bears immediate positive results: Leo can sleep; he doesn’t even need that white-noise machine.
But White Noise is neither particularly funny nor incisive as Parks delivers her critique of empty “woke” platitudes and cultural appropriation with all the subtlety of a blunderbuss.
Exceptional talent – Suzan-Lori Parks wrote it, and Oskar Eustis directs, and Daveed Diggs headlines — combine for a near perfect production at the Public.
It’s a raw rare treat to be challenged at this high level of wise wit and clarity, and for that, I am truly grateful.
The combination makes her latest effort particularly potent theater.
White Noise has many interesting, even compelling scenes; it may even be the first mainstream play to include actual bowling.

cn.t: Parks' provocative play about race and slavery earns strong praise for its daring premise and Daveed Diggs' magnetic performance, though critics split on whether its ambitious ideas cohere into a fully satisfying drama.
